importance.justification: The second atomic weapon used in warfare, destroying northern Nagasaki, causing tens of thousands of deaths, accelerating Japan's surrender in World War II, and marking the beginning of the nuclear weapons era.

title: Atomic bombing of Nagasaki
summary: On 9 August 1945, the United States dropped a plutonium atomic bomb on Nagasaki, detonating over the Urakami district. The blast and radiation killed an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 people by year's end and accelerated Japan's surrender.
card: Three days after Hiroshima, the American B-29 bomber Bockscar diverted from its cloud-covered primary target of Kokura and dropped the Fat Man plutonium bomb over northern Nagasaki at 11:02 a.m. The detonation obliterated the Urakami district, destroyed the landmark Urakami Cathedral, and unleashed catastrophic flash burns, blast trauma, and acute radiation sickness across the civilian population. Combined with the Soviet entry into the war, the destruction forced Emperor Hirohito and the Japanese leadership to announce unconditional surrender on 15 August 1945.
what:
On the morning of 9 August 1945, the United States Army Air Forces B-29 Superfortress Bockscar dropped the second operational nuclear weapon, codenamed Fat Man, over the Japanese port city of Nagasaki. The primary target had been the city of Kokura, but heavy cloud cover and industrial smoke obscured the aiming point across three separate bombing runs. Low on fuel, pilot Major Charles Sweeney and weaponeer Commander Frederick Ashworth diverted southwest to their secondary target of Nagasaki. Finding overcast skies there as well, the crew identified a fleeting visual rift in the cloud layer over the Urakami industrial valley and released the bomb at 11:02 a.m. local time.

The weapon, an implosion-type plutonium-239 bomb with an explosive yield of approximately 21 kilotons, detonated at an altitude of 503 meters directly above a tennis court in Matsuyama-machi. The hypocenter lay in the northern Urakami basin, roughly midway between the Mitsubishi Steel and Arms Works and the Mitsubishi-Urakami Ordnance Works. The thermal flash ignited widespread fires, while the atmospheric shockwave pulverized all wooden structures within one kilometer. Landmarks throughout the valley were annihilated, including the Urakami Cathedral, then the largest Christian church in East Asia, where a priest and parishioners perished beneath collapsing masonry.

Casualty figures remain subject to historical disagreement because wartime municipal rosters burned, entire households died together, and thousands of uncounted Korean forced labourers were present: early Manhattan Project surveys counted only 39,000 dead, whereas the Nagasaki City Atomic Bomb Records Preservation Committee recorded 73,884 fatalities, and modern epidemiological consensus from the Radiation Effects Research Foundation estimates between 60,000 and 80,000 acute deaths by the end of 1945. Surviving victims, known as hibakusha, suffered prolonged medical complications, including severe keloid scarring, leukemia, secondary solid cancers, and lifelong social stigmatization.

uncertainty.note: Detonation timed precisely to 11:02 a.m. JST (02:02 UTC) on 9 August 1945; acute casualty window tracked through end of 1945 (two to four months post-detonation).

how: The bombing was executed by the 509th Composite Group under directives authorized by President Harry S. Truman to enforce the terms of the Potsdam Declaration. (1) Flight and diversion: Bockscar departed Tinian carrying the Fat Man plutonium weapon, but failed to visually acquire Kokura after three runs due to cloud and haze. With fuel diminishing rapidly, the aircraft flew to Nagasaki. (2) Target acquisition and release: Although Nagasaki was also clouded, a fleeting visual break between the Mitsubishi sports field and the steel works permitted visual targeting; the bomb was released from 9,600 meters. (3) Physical blast dynamics: The plutonium implosion created a fireball that expanded to several hundred meters, producing a shockwave with overpressures exceeding several pounds per square inch and ground temperatures reaching thousands of degrees Celsius. (4) Valley confinement: Unlike the flat delta of Hiroshima, Nagasaki's steep mountain ridges confined the explosive blast primarily within the Urakami Valley, sparing the southern port district from total devastation while completely pulverizing the northern sector. (5) Aftermath: Firestorms consumed surviving wooden structures, secondary radiation contaminated soil and water, and emergency rescue personnel entering the ruins received acute secondary doses.
why_it_matters: The atomic bombing of Nagasaki, occurring hours after the Soviet Red Army invaded Japanese-occupied Manchuria, served as the final military shock that fractured the resistance of the Japanese Supreme War Council. Combined with Hiroshima, it demonstrated that the United States possessed an ongoing atomic arsenal capable of systematic urban destruction, convincing Emperor Hirohito to intervene directly and broadcast Japan's surrender on 15 August 1945, bringing World War II to an immediate close without an Allied amphibious invasion of the home islands. The biological toll transformed medical understanding of ionizing radiation: the Life Span Study conducted by the Radiation Effects Research Foundation tracked hundreds of thousands of hibakusha across generations, establishing global standards for radiological protection and occupational exposure limits. In geopolitical history, Nagasaki remains the last occasion on which a nuclear weapon was detonated in armed conflict. The horrific suffering of its victims galvanized the international nuclear disarmament movement, centered upon the hibakusha motto that Nagasaki must remain the last city to experience atomic warfare. Had Bockscar aborted its mission and returned to Okinawa without dropping the weapon, or had Soviet entry occurred without a second atomic strike, the Imperial Japanese Army might have prolonged resistance into the autumn, triggering the bloody invasion envisioned under Operation Downfall and costing hundreds of thousands of additional military and civilian lives.

perspectives.holder: United States Government / President Harry S. Truman
perspectives.account: The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, executed in conjunction with the Potsdam ultimatum, were necessary military operations to compel Japan's unconditional surrender, avert an amphibious invasion of the home islands, and avoid heavy Allied and Japanese casualties.

perspectives.holder: Revisionist and diplomatic historians (e.g. Tsuyoshi Hasegawa, Gar Alperovitz)
perspectives.account: The Soviet declaration of war and invasion of Manchuria on 9 August was the primary catalyst breaking the deadlock in Tokyo, making the second atomic strike on Nagasaki militarily superfluous and hastily executed before Japanese leadership could react to Hiroshima.

perspectives.holder: Hibakusha and Nagasaki peace movement (Nagasaki Peace Declaration, survivor testimonies)
perspectives.account: The atomic bombings were catastrophic atrocities directed against civilian populations that inflicted acute trauma, generational radiation illnesses, and lasting psychological injury, demonstrating that nuclear weapons are incompatible with human survival and must be completely abolished.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the exact total death toll (RERF range of 60,000–80,000 acute deaths vs Nagasaki City committee count of 73,884), as wartime municipal rosters were destroyed and thousands of unrecorded Korean forced labourers were present.
parent_reconciliation: Parent record 1939-world-war-ii records total worldwide civilian deaths of 45 million and total wartime mortality of 70 to 85 million. Nagasaki's acute casualties (60,000–80,000 deaths by the end of 1945 according to RERF, or 73,884 according to the Nagasaki City committee) represent a localized component of the Pacific War civilian casualties included in the global wartime total.
